archetype.name: Playoff Team (ball-control, record slightly flattered)
archetype.definition: A genuinely good, top-ten-efficiency team that wins by holding the ball and choking third downs, though its 7-2 record runs about two wins ahead of how it has actually played.

report.headline: A real playoff team, but 7-2 overstates it: winning despite the turnovers.
report.take:
In Ben Johnson's second year, Chicago plays a possession game. The Bears hold the ball a league-best 34.52 minutes a game, gain 384.3 yards a game (third), and their offense's 47.1% success rate ranks seventh. The other side does the same job: opponents convert just 22.8% of third downs, the best mark in the league, and the defense's 40.8% success rate allowed ranks fourth. The result is a team that controls games on the field, at a net EPA of 0.081 (ninth). That is good, not dominant, and it is the honest baseline for this club.

The record is a notch better than that baseline, and it got there oddly. Usually a team ahead of its numbers is winning the turnover battle. These Bears have given the ball away 17 times, sit at -4 in turnover margin, and rank 29th at -0.9 a game. They won anyway by going 0.75 in one-score games, getting 3.23 EPA a game from special teams (fourth), and grinding out drives. Their point differential implies 5 wins, not 7, which is where the 2 wins over expected come from. Last year's 11-win team was flattered by a league-best +1.3 turnover margin behind a 21st-ranked defense. This year's team is built more soundly and has been less lucky with the ball, but luckier in close finishes.

The raw season numbers blur two things. First, the quarterback split: Caleb Williams missed Weeks 3 through 5. Case Keenum won both of his starts against weak offenses, and Tyson Bagent's 7-31 loss in Green Bay, with five turnovers, is the worst game on the sheet. The 59-37 opener in Carolina also inflates the scoring average. Second, the defense has a split personality. It is suffocating underneath, at -0.205 EPA on short passes (second) with 26 sacks (third), and porous over the top, at 1.325 EPA on deep balls (31st) with explosive passes allowed at a 24th-ranked rate. That deep-ball problem now meets a cornerback room with Malik Muhammad II out and Tyrique Stevenson Sr. nursing a hand injury.

Where it goes from here depends on the schedule more than on anything about Chicago. After New Orleans comes the hardest closing stretch imaginable: Detroit twice, Jacksonville, Buffalo on the road, Green Bay, and a finale in Minnesota, with four division games in a race where all four teams have six or seven wins. The turnover rate should drift back toward normal, which helps. The close-game magic probably won't hold, which hurts. Those roughly cancel. This looks like a 10-to-11-win team that makes the playoffs and has a coin-flip shot at the division.

strengths.title: Possession football on both sides
strengths.body: The Bears lead the league in time of possession and rank third in yards a game, because the offense stays on schedule (seventh in success rate) and the defense gets off the field on third down better than anyone. Long drives keep their own defense fresh and shorten games against better opponents. This is structural, a product of scheme and down-to-down efficiency rather than big plays, so it should travel.

strengths.title: A pass rush that finishes
strengths.body: Chicago has 26 sacks, third in the league, on an 8.6% sack rate, even though its pressure rate is only eighth. That gap means the rush converts pressure into sacks efficiently. Paired with tight underneath coverage, it makes long third downs nearly hopeless for opponents. Losing DT Kentavius Street to IR thins the rotation, but he was a 41%-snap player, so the core rush is intact.

strengths.title: Protection that buys time
strengths.body: Williams and the backups hold the ball longer than any quarterbacks in the league, 3.191 seconds to throw, yet the line allows pressure at just 17.2% (sixth) and QB hits at a fifth-ranked rate. Johnson's offense lets routes develop downfield because the front holds up. The test is whether that survives losing left tackle Braxton Jones for the season.

concerns.title: Giving the ball away too often
concerns.body: Seventeen turnovers in nine games is a real flaw, not just noise. Two games had five each: Bagent's loss in Green Bay and Williams's narrow escape against Tampa Bay. Some of it is the cost of an aggressive, hold-the-ball passing game, but the 2025 team was +1.3 a game, so these quarterbacks are capable of protecting it. Expect improvement, though not a full reversal.

concerns.title: Deep balls beat this defense
concerns.body: The defense takes away everything short and pays for it over the top. Deep-pass EPA allowed ranks 31st, and the explosive pass rate allowed ranks 24th. New England threw for 321 and Carolina for 361. With Muhammad out and Stevenson hurt, the weakest part of the defense is now also its thinnest. Against Buffalo, Detroit and Jacksonville, this is the likeliest way they lose.

concerns.title: Record runs ahead of the margin
concerns.body: A 0.75 one-score win rate and 2 wins over expected mean the point differential supports a 5-win team so far, not a 7-win one. Close-game records rarely hold. With the schedule stiffening, a couple of those coin flips will likely go the other way.

trend.note: Since Williams returned in Week 6, the Bears have won every game, with positive passing EPA until the five-turnover scare against Tampa Bay. Before that, the quarterback carousel produced swings from 27-7 to 7-31.

nextGame.headline: Rested Bears get a Saints defense that can't pressure or cover deep
nextGame.body:
Chicago comes off its bye with 14 days of rest and hosts a 3-5 New Orleans team that ranks 26th in net EPA. The Saints' defense fits this offense badly. It generates pressure at just 16.8% (31st), allows 1.545 EPA on deep passes (dead last), and lets opponents convert 47.2% of third downs (28th). For a passing game that holds the ball longer than anyone, a defense that can't get home is an invitation. The Saints' offense, with Tyler Shough starting every game, ranks 22nd in EPA and runs poorly: 3.29 yards a carry and a 33.3% run success rate, 31st. Expect New Orleans to go for it on fourth down, since it has converted every attempt this year, but its route to points will have to come through the air.

Availability tilts toward Chicago. For the Bears, Muhammad is listed out with a return estimate of game day, Stevenson is questionable with a hand injury, top target Luther Burden III is in the concussion protocol, backup back Kyle Monangai is out, and Jones is gone for the year. The corner and Burden statuses are the ones to track this week. For the Saints, center Erik McCoy, a 97%-snap starter, will be out "for a little bit" with a biceps injury. Travis Etienne Jr. is on IR without his practice window opened, and CJ Donaldson is out, which leaves an already weak run game thin at back and up front.

waysToWin.title: Clean pockets, shots downfield
waysToWin.body: New Orleans barely pressures and is the league's worst deep-ball defense, while Chicago's line keeps its passers clean. With time to throw, Williams should find the intermediate and deep throws that tight coverage usually takes away. If Burden can't go, Rome Odunze and Kalif Raymond inherit those looks.

waysToWin.title: Feed Loveland in the middle
waysToWin.body: Offenses throw to tight ends more often than usual against New Orleans, and those targets produce 0.44 EPA a play, 28th in the league. Colston Loveland is Chicago's second-most targeted receiver and a natural pressure valve if Burden is limited.

waysToWin.title: Make the Saints one-dimensional
waysToWin.body: The Bears' weak spot against lead backs matters less when the Saints are down to their depth backs behind a line missing its center. If Chicago wins early downs, Shough faces third-and-long against the league's best third-down defense and a rush that finishes sacks.

waysToLose.title: Another turnover-fest
waysToLose.body: The cleanest way for a 3-5 team to steal this game is with extra possessions and short fields. Chicago coughed it up five times against Tampa Bay and survived only barely. Repeating that at home against a team with nothing to lose would erase every efficiency edge.

waysToLose.title: Shough hits the shorthanded secondary deep
waysToLose.body: New Orleans can't run, so it will throw, and the place to throw against Chicago is deep. With Muhammad and Stevenson both uncertain, a few completions down the field could keep the Saints in a game the Bears should control.

waysToLose.title: Flags stall the drives
waysToLose.body: At 8 penalties a game (23rd), Chicago gives back yardage, and its ball-control approach depends on staying ahead of the chains. The 133 penalty yards in Atlanta show how a sloppy day can turn sustained drives into punts.

nextGame.watch: Williams's ball security after the five-turnover night against Tampa Bay: with a clean pocket likely, any giveaways will be self-inflicted.

restOfSeason.body:
The foundation is sustainable. Possession dominance, third-down defense, a finishing pass rush and sound protection come from scheme and personnel, not bounces. Turnovers should come down from a 29th-ranked rate, which is real upside. Against that, a 0.75 one-score record and 2 wins over expected tend to regress, and the schedule after New Orleans is as hard as it gets. Detroit, Buffalo and Jacksonville all have top-seven offenses that can exploit the deep-ball weakness, and Minnesota's top-ranked defense already held Chicago to 3 points.

Realistically, the Saints and Miami are the clear wins left. The rest are near coin flips, and four of them decide a division packed tight at the top. Expect slightly fewer points than the opener-inflated average suggests and similar points allowed, with the corner injuries the biggest swing. A wild-card berth is the likely floor if Williams stays healthy. The division depends on splitting the Detroit pair and winning at least one of the Green Bay and Minnesota games.
swingFactors: Cornerback health against deep passing offenses
Results in four remaining division games

confidence.note: Nine games, three of them with backup quarterbacks, plus key secondary injuries.
